The strongest signal was your third-year class standing. You finished in the first decile, the lowest tenth of your class, while accepted students were, on average, around the sixth decile. This pointed firmly toward failing the bar. Your first-year class standing had the next largest effect, and it told the same story: also in the first decile, near the bottom, and that further increased your predicted risk.

The third factor was your LSAT score. At 32, it was below the average of about 37 for admitted students. This also pushed the prediction toward failure, but it was less influential than your class rankings. Together, these three factors all moved in the same direction, producing the high failure probability.
